patient_note_history:
History 
HPI: A 54-year-old male presents for follow-up of his hypertension that was diagnosed last year. He was initially started on HCTZ; propranolol was added 6 months ago. He is fairly compliant with his medications. He does not monitor his blood pressure at home. His last blood pressure checkup was 6 months ago. He is feeling well except for erectile dysfunction and decreased libido noted 4 months ago. No leg claudication or any previous history of heart problems, stroke, TIA, or diabetes. No marital or work problems. No depression, anxiety, appetite or weight changes, or history of trauma. 
ROS: Negative except as above. 
Allergies: NKDA. 
Medications: HCTZ, propranolol, lovastatin. 
PMH: Hypertension, hypercholesterolemia diagnosed 1 year ago. 
PSH: No, I do not. 
SH: No smoking, 3-4 beers/week, no illicit drugs. Works as a schoolteacher; married and lives with his wife. 
FH: Father died of a heart attack at age 50. Mother is in a nursing home due to Alzheimer's disease.

exam_lines.source_text: Patient is in no acute distress.
Neck: No carotid bruits, no jugular venous distention.
Chest: Clear breath sounds bilaterally. No gynecomastia.
Heart: Apical impulse not displaced; regular rate and rhythm; heart sounds within normal limits; no murmurs, rubs, or gallops.
Abdomen: Soft, non-distended, non-tender, normal bowel sounds x 4 quadrants, no bruits, no organomegaly.
Extremities: No edema, no hair loss or skin changes. Radial, brachial, femoral, dorsalis pedis, and posterior tibialis 2+ and symmetric.

Neuro: Motor strength grade 5/5 in bilateral lower extremities. Sensation: Intact to pinprick and soft touch in lower extremities. Deep tendon reflexes: Symmetric grade 2+ in lower extremities, bilateral Babinski sign present.

gold_target:
Diagnosis #1: Medication-induced erectile dysfunction 
History Finding(s): 
- Taking propranolol 
- Onset of erectile dysfunction coincides with propranolol use
- No early-morning or nocturnal tumescence

Physical Exam Finding(s): None

Diagnosis #2: Erectile dysfunction secondary to vascular disease 
History Finding(s): 
- History of hypertension 
- History of hyperlipidemia 
- No early-morning or nocturnal tumescence 

Physical Exam Finding(s): None

Diagnosis #3: Hypogonadism 
History Finding(s): 
- Loss of libido and ED 
- Hair loss 
- No early-morning or nocturnal tumescence 

Physical Exam Finding(s): None
gold_additional_diagnosis:
• Depression: Psychogenic causes can lead to a loss of libido and loss of erections and are suggested when 
nocturnal or early morning erections are preserved (not seen in this case). This patient denies other depressive 
symptoms, but further exploration of his feelings about his nursing home-bound mother may be more revealing. 
• Peyronie's disease: Fibrous plaque of the tunica albuginea can lead to penile scarring and ED.
raw_opening:
Opening Scenario:

James Miller, a 50-year-old male, comes to the clinic for a hypertension follow-up.

Vital Signs:

- BP: 135/88 mmHg
- Temp: 98.0°F (36.7°C)
- RR: 16/minute
- HR: 70/minute, regular

Examinee Tasks:

1. Take a focused history.
2. Perform a focused physical exam (do not perform rectal, genitourinary, or female breast exam).
3. Explain your clinical impression and workup plan to the patient.
4. Write the patient note after leaving the room.

Checklist/SP Sheet:

Patient Description:

The patient is a 54-year-old male who appears anxious.

Notes for the SP:

- Don't mention impotence unless the examinee asks whether you are having any side effects from your medications or whether you have any other concerns.

Challenging Questions to Ask:

""I've begun to encounter issues with my sexual performance, which I believe are related to my age. Is that correct, doctor?"

Examinee Response:

"I don't believe your age is the cause.". I worry more about your medications. Testosterone levels may decline with aging, and we will monitor for this.."

Examinee Checklist:

Entrance:

- The examinee knocked on the door before entering.
- The examinee made eye contact with the SP.
- The examinee correctly used the patient's name.
- The examinee introduced themselves by name.
- The examinee identified their role or position.

Reflective Listening:

- The examinee asked an open-ended question and actively listened to the response.
- The examinee asked the SP to list his/her concerns and listened to the response without interrupting.
- The examinee summarized the SP's concerns, often using the SP's own words.

Information Gathering:

The examinee elicited data efficiently and accurately.

Connecting With the Patient:

The examinee recognized the SP's emotions and responded with PEARLS.

Physical Examination:

- Examinee washed their hands.
- Examinee asked permission to start the exam.
- Examinee used respectful draping.
- Examinee did not repeat painful maneuvers.

Exam Component Maneuver:

- Head and neck exam: Fundoscopic exam, carotid auscultation.
- Cardiovascular exam: Palpation, auscultation.
- Pulmonary exam: Auscultation.
- Abdominal exam: Auscultation, palpation.
- Extremities exam: Palpation of peripheral pulses.
- Neurological exam: Deep tendon reflexes (DTRs), Babinski sign, sensation, and strength in bilateral lower extremities.

Sample Closure:

"Mr. Miller, your blood pressure level was 135/88 when we measured it earlier today, which is close to our target of 130/80. However, it would be even better if we could get it down to around 120/80. Fortunately, achieving this is attainable by implementing lifestyle modifications, including reducing your salt and fat consumption and initiating regular exercise.. Even half an hour of walking can make a huge difference. 

As for your problems with your erection, this is a very common side effect of one of the blood pressure medications you are taking. Therefore, I would like to prescribe you a different medication besides propranolol to manage your blood pressure.. I will also request some blood tests to rule out other potential medical conditions contributing to your issue.. In addition, I would like to perform a genital exam as well as a rectal exam to assess your prostate. Do you have any questions for me?"

Closure:

- Examinee discussed initial diagnostic impressions.
- Examinee discussed initial management plans.
  - Follow-up tests: Examinee mentioned the need for genital and rectal exams.
  - Lifestyle modification (diet, exercise, alcohol cessation).
  - Changing propranolol to another antihypertensive medication that does not cause erectile dysfunction.
- Examinee asked if the SP had any other questions or concerns.Patient Note:
